summary.text: Take \(n=7\): every allowed value of \(x\) is at least \(3\), and \(x\le y\le z\) therefore forces \(x+y+z\ge 3+3+3=9\), contradicting the required sum \(7\). Thus the strengthened representation claim already fails at \(n=7\), independently of the primality conditions.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]
The conjecture is a conjunction of two universally asserted properties: first, that the counting function \(a(n)\) is positive for every \(n>5\); and second, that for every \(n>6\) there are positive integers \(x,y,z\) satisfying
\[
x+y+z=n,\qquad x\le y\le z,\qquad x\in S,
\]
together with the stated primality conditions on
\[
2x-1,\ 2y-1,\ 2z-1,\ 2xy-1,\ 2xz-1,\ 2yz-1.
\]
It is enough to disprove the second universal assertion, since a conjunction is false if either one of its clauses is false.

Take \(n=7\). Certainly \(7>6\), so the “moreover” clause would provide positive integers \(x,y,z\) such that
\[
x+y+z=7,\qquad x\le y\le z,\qquad x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\},
\]
as well as all six primality conditions.

Membership in the displayed finite set gives the exhaustive alternatives
\[
x=3,\quad x=4,\quad x=6,\quad x=10,\quad\text{or}\quad x=15.
\]
In every one of these cases, \(x\ge 3\). Since \(x\le y\), it follows that \(y\ge 3\). Since \(y\le z\), it follows in turn that \(z\ge 3\). Consequently
\[
x+y+z\ge 3+3+3=9.
\]
This contradicts the required equality \(x+y+z=7\).

Equivalently, the individual alternatives can be seen directly: if \(x=3\), ordering forces the sum to be at least \(3+3+3=9\); if \(x=4\), it is at least \(12\); if \(x=6\), at least \(18\); if \(x=10\), at least \(30\); and if \(x=15\), at least \(45\). Thus no allowed value of \(x\) can occur in an ordered triple summing to \(7\). The primality requirements never even arise, because the elementary size and ordering requirements are already inconsistent.

Therefore the required representation does not exist for \(n=7>6\). Hence the strengthened universal clause is false, and so the combined conjecture is false.

For completeness, this counterexample concerns the strengthened clause rather than positivity of the sequence at \(7\): indeed, \(7=2+2+3\), and for this ordered triple the six relevant numbers are
\[
2\cdot2-1=3,\quad 2\cdot2-1=3,\quad 2\cdot3-1=5,
\]
and
\[
2\cdot2\cdot2-1=7,\quad 2\cdot2\cdot3-1=11,\quad 2\cdot2\cdot3-1=11,
\]
all of which are prime. Thus \(a(7)>0\), but in its ordered form the triple has least entry \(2\), which is not in \(S\). This does not rescue the conjecture: its assertion that every \(n>6\) has an ordered representation whose first entry lies in \(S\) already fails at \(n=7\).
